revisions.title: The third war: Athens conquered by no one but Athens
revisions.body: The third war begins as an unexpected and terrible turn in the catalogue, moving through the Sicilian and Hellespont campaigns. The orator then names the shocking escalation: other Greeks summoned the Persian king—once expelled with Athens—against the city and gathered Greeks and barbarians for the attack. At Mytilene, sixty Athenian ships rescue the trapped fleet, defeat the enemy, and free their friends; the fallen rescuers make the city's strength and virtue visible. Their achievement gives Athens a reputation for never being conquered, and the orator says that reputation proved true. The defeat that follows is assigned inward: Athens was overcome by its own dissension, not by others. It remained unconquered by external enemies, yet it both defeated and was defeated by itself; after peace with the others, the conflict becomes the city's own war.

revisions.title: The city as heir, father, and guardian — then the dismissal
revisions.body: The closing movement places the city in familial roles toward the war dead and their families: heir and son to the dead, father to their sons, and guardian to their parents. It also describes the city's continuing care through annual customary rites and athletic, equestrian, and musical contests. After urging the mourners to bear their loss more gently, the speaker gives the final procedural command: having joined in lament, they are to depart.
